b: Bid density is the number of bids submitted for a single ad impression in a programmatic auction. It is a measure of competition. An impression that draws eight bids is denser than one that draws two, and in most auction designs the denser impression clears at a higher price, because the winner has to beat more rivals. The term exists because publishers, supply-side platforms (SSPs) and buyers needed shorthand for what fill rates do not capture: not whether an impression sold, but how many buyers wanted it.

No standards body owns a formal definition. The Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB) Tech Lab does not specify it in OpenRTB, and the closest entry in the IAB UK jargon buster is "bid rate", which it describes as a metric that "shows how many Bids are occurring in the Auction." The phrase is trade vocabulary, used with slightly different meanings by different companies.

A programmatic auction starts when a page or app has an ad slot to fill. The publisher's wrapper or ad server sends bid requests to SSPs, which forward them to demand-side platforms (DSPs). Each DSP decides, usually in well under a second, whether to return a price or nothing.
Bid density is what is left after those decisions. In its simplest form it is calculated as:
bids received ÷ impressions auctioned (average bids per impression), or
bids received ÷ bid requests sent (sometimes reported as a bid rate).

The two versions produce very different numbers. A publisher that sends one impression to 15 SSPs, each of which forwards it to dozens of DSPs, can generate hundreds of requests for one slot. Five bids then look healthy per impression and negligible per request, so any comparison has to start with the denominator.

A worked example shows why density matters for revenue. Under a second-price auction, the winner pays roughly one increment above the second-highest bid. In a 2018 column for AdExchanger, Michael Necheporenko, chief technology officer of Roxot, described a $3.00 winning bid against a $1.50 runner-up: the winner pays about $1.50, so half of the winning bid is surplus the publisher never sees. Add a third bidder at $2.80 and the clearing price nearly doubles. Under a first-price auction, the winner pays its own bid, but density still matters: buyers using bid shading algorithms lower their bids when they predict little competition, and raise them when they expect a crowded auction.

Several protocol features feed the number. OpenRTB, the IAB Tech Lab's real-time bidding protocol, allows a bid response to contain multiple seat bids, each with multiple bid objects, so one DSP can in principle submit more than one price. On the client side, Prebid.js offers a MultiBid module that, according to Prebid documentation, lets configured bidders "pass more than one bid per AdUnit through to the ad server." The maxBids setting caps this at nine, and extra bids are passed to the ad server under prefixed key-values such as hb_pb_PREFIX2 only if a targetBiddercodePrefix is set. Without the module, only the highest bid from each bidder is considered.

On the sell side, publishers watch bid density in wrapper analytics and SSP reports to decide which demand partners to keep, how high to set price floors, and when to stop calling partners that never bid. On the buy side, DSPs see how many offered impressions they bid on, and how often the same impression arrives through several routes.

Typical values are low. Freestar, a header-bidding vendor, wrote in July 2025 that bid density "is typically quite low" and that, according to unnamed industry data, fewer than 10% of available DSP seats bid on a given impression, sometimes as few as 1% to 3%. Benjamin Hansz of Rivr put the share of unanswered requests "above 90% of most bidstreams" in a 2023 interview, cited in PPC Land's explainer on traffic shaping. Necheporenko's 2018 analysis found an average SSP bid on only 40% to 50% of available inventory, and "only two to three bidders competed" in many header auctions.

The concept predates the label: in second-price exchanges, the gap between the top two bids set publisher revenue, so thin competition was always costly. What changed was header bidding, which spread in the mid-2010s and let publishers send one impression to several exchanges at once instead of through a sequential waterfall.

The phrase was in trade circulation by 2017. PubMatic's 2017 primer on auction dynamics described dynamic floors as a way to "simulate bid density" by adding a synthetic second price to thin auctions, pushing them "closer to first price." The same paper warned that parallel requests meant each SSP and DSP was "receiving more traffic while filling smaller percentages of inventory." In August 2017, PPC Land's comparison of client-side and server-to-server header bidding presented server-side setups as offering "less latency and better bid density."

The shift to first-price auctions changed what density meant for prices. Google announced on March 6, 2019 that Ad Manager would move to a unified first-price auction, and on September 5, 2019 said the full rollout would complete "over the next few weeks." Google also said it planned a Bid Data Transfer file showing publishers "the range and number of bids" they received, which turned bid counts into a standard reporting field rather than a vendor metric.

From around 2020 the problem inverted. Publishers had added so many SSPs, and SSPs so many reselling relationships, that DSPs were flooded with duplicate requests. According to AdExchanger's report of a September 2024 talk by Chris Kane, founder of Jounce Media, web publishers start roughly 30 million auctions per second while the average DSP listens to about 3 million queries per second (QPS). DSPs responded by throttling and filtering, cutting the bids any single publisher could expect.

For publishers, bid density is close to a direct proxy for yield. The fight over transaction IDs in 2025 showed how closely the two are tied. On August 27, 2025, Prebid.org disabled the cross-exchange function of transaction IDs, the identifiers DSPs used to recognise the same impression arriving through multiple SSPs. PPC Land's coverage noted that some publishers had "benefited from auction duplication as it increased their effective yield," and the IAB Tech Lab said the change risked undermining the OpenRTB specification.

Raptive then proposed encrypted transaction IDs paired with mandatory multi-bidding. Paul Bannister, Raptive's chief strategy officer, said: "Multi-bidding will replace some of the bid density that will be lost from transaction IDs being available." If DSPs can see that five requests are one impression, they bid once, and publishers want a structured way to recover that competition.
For advertisers, density is the other side of cost: more competition means higher clearing prices, and some of it is the same buyer reaching the impression through different paths.

The first problem is definitional. Some sources count bids per impression; others count bid events, including several bids from one advertiser across creatives. A November 2026 retail media glossary entry from Racklify separated "auction density", the number of competing advertisers, from bid density, the volume of bidding activity, and warned that heavy bidding from a small set of advertisers can cause "clearing price instability."

The second is that density can be manufactured. Duplicate requests, multi-bidding and resold auctions all raise the count of bids without adding a new buyer. Dynamic floors, as PubMatic described them, simulate density rather than create it.

Third, vendor figures are hard to verify. At an IAB Europe event on July 3, 2025, Filippo Gramigna, co-chief executive of OneTag, said curation had produced an increase in bid density of up to 40%, translating into a 25% to 30% revenue gain for publishers. Other panellists offered no comparable data. Necheporenko argued in 2018 that about half of header bidding's revenue lift came from fewer unfilled impressions rather than extra competition, which cuts against the assumption that more bidders explain most gains.

Finally, the Media Rating Council's draft auction transparency standards, released in September 2025, encourage multi-bid and transaction ID support but do not require disclosure of how many bids an auction received. Bid density remains largely self-reported.
Fill rate measures whether an impression sold at all (impressions served divided by ad requests). An auction with one bid and one with ten both count as filled.
Ad density is unrelated to auctions: it measures how much of a page is covered by ads, a concern for the Coalition for Better Ads and for made-for-advertising site classifications.
Win rate is a buyer metric: the share of bids a DSP submits that win.
Auction density, where used, counts distinct competing advertisers rather than bids.

Live streaming made bid density an engineering problem. Disney Advertising's certification for programmatic live streaming, announced in January 2025, required partners to cope with sudden audience spikes while maintaining increased bid density. When Magnite launched Live Scheduler on November 18, 2025, PPC Land's coverage recalled that the certification demanded bid density management during peak viewership, and the term resurfaced in March 2026 analysis of Magnite's preparation for the 2026 football tournament.

The open web's traffic decline has raised a different question: whether there will be enough impressions to bid on. PPC Land's August 2026 analysis of Amazon's DSP consolidation argued that "no bid density survives the disappearance of the page" as AI answers absorb search referrals. And today, Criteo's guide to advertising in AI chat interfaces was reported to pitch publishers on improving bid density and CPMs.

Who: Publishers, SSPs and wrapper vendors track bid density on the sell side; DSPs see it from the buy side. Prebid.org, the IAB Tech Lab, the Media Rating Council and companies such as Raptive, OneTag, Magnite and Disney Advertising have shaped recent debate over it.

What: The number of bids an ad impression receives in a programmatic auction, used as a measure of competition. It has no formal standard definition, and sources differ on whether to count bids per impression, per request or per advertiser.

When: The underlying concern dates from second-price exchanges in the late 2000s; the phrase was in trade use by 2017 with the spread of header bidding, gained new weight after Google's 2019 move to first-price auctions, and returned to the centre of debate with the transaction ID dispute of August and September 2025.

Where: In open web display, video and app auctions running through header bidding wrappers, SSPs and ad servers, and increasingly in connected TV (CTV) and live streaming, where audience spikes stress bidding capacity.

Why: Denser auctions generally clear at higher prices, so bid density is closely tied to publisher revenue. It is contested because duplicate requests, multi-bidding and resold auctions can inflate it without adding real buyers, while DSP throttling and deduplication can reduce it.
